turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. I, uh, I came in because I'm just having a really hard time at work lately. I'm a high school teacher, and I'll sit down at my desk with a huge stack of essays to grade, or maybe a new curriculum document, fully intending to just power through and get it done. 

Actually, I teach history, mostly sophomores this year, which is just a wild age. Lately they're obsessed with this weird TikTok trend where they try to subtly incorporate pop song lyrics into their historical analysis papers. I caught one kid doing it with Taylor Swift last week—he managed to get "Anti-Hero" into an essay about the Cold War, which honestly was pretty clever, I had to hand it to him. But... wait, what was I saying? 

Oh, right, the grading. So I'll sit down to grade those essays, and within ten minutes I'll realize I’ve just been staring at the exact same page. Like, I haven't actually read a single word. I'm just sitting there thinking about three other completely different things—like that kid's essay, or what I need to get at the grocery store—and I'm barely taking in what's right in front of me. It's just getting impossible to get through my work.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to maintain focus on work tasks like grading essays for more than ten minutes.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient reports being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts, such as grocery lists or student anecdotes, while trying to work.

turns.doctor_question: Have you struggled with this kind of difficulty staying focused or getting tasks finished for most of your life, even when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, honestly, it's been like this for as long as I can remember. Even back in primary school, my parents would always find these crumpled-up worksheets shoved at the bottom of my backpack that I’d just completely forgotten to turn in. I remember my mom getting so mad about this one time I had a diorama due—it was on the solar system, and I had spent hours painting these little foam balls. I was so proud of Jupiter, I even gave it the Great Red Spot and everything. But then I just... left it on the kitchen counter. For three days. 

And my report cards were always full of the same comments, year after year. The teachers would write things like, "bright but careless," or they'd say I wouldn't finish my work unless someone was standing right over me, watching me do it. Which reminds me, the principal at that school was this guy Mr. Henderson, and he had this enormous mustache that looked exactly like a walrus. We used to make jokes about it constantly... but yeah, the focus thing has definitely been a lifelong struggle, not just a recent thing.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient recalls teachers describing them as 'bright but careless,' indicating a history of careless mistakes.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly confirms that 'the focus thing has definitely been a lifelong struggle.'
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient mentions they 'wouldn't finish my work unless someone was standing right over me,' showing difficulty following through and finishing schoolwork.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes having 'crumpled-up worksheets shoved at the bottom of my backpack,' which points to difficulty organizing materials.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility during the interview by going on an unrelated tangent about their former principal's mustache.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient describes frequently forgetting to turn in completed homework and leaving a school project on the counter for days.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often feel like you are driven by a motor, or do you find yourself constantly needing to be on the go?
turns.patient_response: No, not really. I'm definitely not one of those people who can't sit still or always has to be doing something. I'm actually pretty happy just lounging around. My husband is the one who's always on the go. He's a physical therapist, so he's literally on his feet all day, and then he comes home and wants to go for a run or do yard work. We just bought this house last year, and the yard was a total disaster—just overgrown weeds everywhere and this weird, rusty old swing set in the back. He's been obsessed with fixing it up. He even started building a raised garden bed last weekend. He wants to plant tomatoes and zucchini, which is great, I love zucchini bread, but I told him we're probably going to end up with way too much zucchini. You know how it is, it just takes over. People always end up trying to give away giant zucchinis to their neighbors... but yeah, no, I don't feel driven by a motor at all. I just sit there. I just sit there and stare at the essays.

symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly denies feeling driven by a motor or constantly needing to be on the go, stating she is happy lounging around.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find that you often interrupt others when they are speaking or find it difficult to wait your turn in conversations?
turns.patient_response: No, I don't think so. I'm usually pretty quiet in conversations, actually. I'm more of a listener, you know? Unless we're talking about something I'm really interested in, like history. My husband says I can talk for hours about the Roman Empire. We went to Italy for our honeymoon a few years ago, and I swear I drove him crazy pointing out every single ruin we walked past. The food there was amazing, though. We had this pasta dish in Rome, cacio e pepe, and it was just so simple but so good. I've tried to make it at home like a dozen times, but it never comes out right. The cheese always clumps up instead of making a smooth sauce. I read somewhere that you have to use a specific type of Pecorino Romano and the starchy pasta water, but... wait, what were we talking about? Interrupting people? Yeah, no, I don't really do that. I usually just kind of zone out while they're talking anyway.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient admits she usually zones out while others are talking to her.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient gets distracted by her own unrelated thoughts about her honeymoon and pasta, completely losing track of the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient denies the doctor's question about having difficulty waiting her turn in conversations.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient explicitly denies interrupting people, stating she is usually quiet and more of a listener.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often find that you lose or misplace things that you need to get your work done, like your keys, phone, or school materials?
turns.patient_response: Oh, absolutely. It's an everyday thing. I’m constantly hunting for things I need for the day, like my classroom keys, my lesson notes, or my USB drive. It’s like, I’ll have them in my hand five minutes earlier, and then they just vanish. It happens a lot with my whistle and cards, too, for when I referee soccer games on the weekends. I love reffing, actually. It's a great way to stay involved in the sport since I don't really have the knees to play competitively anymore. I tore my ACL back in college playing intramurals. It was the worst. I was just going up for a header and landed completely wrong. The rehab took forever, and the physical therapist I went to was this guy who always played the worst 80s hair metal bands during my sessions. Like, I appreciate a little Def Leppard now and then, but every single Tuesday and Thursday at 4 PM? It was a lot. But yeah, I actually had to buy a backup whistle because I kept leaving my main one in random places, like on top of the microwave or in the cup holder of my wife's car. It's incredibly frustrating because I know I just had it, but I just can't keep track of my stuff.

symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly confirms constantly losing necessary items for work and hobbies, such as classroom keys, lesson notes, USB drives, and refereeing equipment.

turns.doctor_question: When you are working on your tasks, do you often make careless mistakes because you have trouble paying close attention to details?
turns.patient_response: Careless mistakes? Um... I don't really know if I'd call them careless, exactly. I mean, I guess I haven't really noticed making a ton of mistakes on the details. I grade so many papers, you know? It's just a constant stream of essays. I teach 10th-grade world history, and right now we're doing the Industrial Revolution. It's actually a fascinating period. The way the textile industry completely shifted society... I have this one lesson where I bring in raw cotton and show them how hard it is to separate the seeds by hand. Most of these kids have no idea where their clothes even come from. They're all just wearing fast fashion, ordering stuff off Shein or whatever. My niece is constantly getting these huge packages delivered. She's 14, and her room is just an absolute disaster zone of cheap clothes. I tried to explain to her the environmental impact of it all, but you know teenagers. They just roll their eyes and put their AirPods back in. But yeah, as far as my own work goes... I don't really think I make a lot of detail mistakes. I just kind of power through the grading as best I can.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly denies making careless or detail-oriented mistakes in her work.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find that you often fidget, tap your hands or feet, or squirm in your seat when you are expected to remain seated for long periods?
turns.patient_response:
Squirming? No, not really. I don't think I'm much of a fidgeter. Even when I have to sit through those awful professional development days at school, I usually just sit there. We always have them in the school library, and the chairs are just those hard plastic ones from the 90s. They are incredibly uncomfortable. Last week we had this three-hour seminar on the new grading software the district is making us use. It's called like, EduTrack or something? Anyway, it's completely counterintuitive. You have to click through four different screens just to enter a single quiz grade. It's a nightmare. 

My colleague Dave, he teaches AP Calc, he was sitting next to me and he *does* fidget. He clicks his pen non-stop. Just click, click, click, the entire time. It drives me absolutely up the wall. I finally had to ask him to put the pen down because I couldn't even hear the presenter. Not that the presenter was saying anything useful anyway. She kept using all these corporate buzzwords like "synergy" and "backward design." I mean, I'm just trying to teach 15-year-olds about the French Revolution, I don't need corporate synergy. We spent a whole month on the French Revolution last year and the kids actually got really into the guillotine stuff. Teenagers are morbid like that. 

But yeah, what did you ask? Oh, if I tap my feet or squirm. No, I usually just sit pretty still. I might completely zone out during those meetings, but I'm not bouncing around in my seat or anything.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient admits to completely zoning out during long meetings, indicating difficulty sustaining attention.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly denies squirming, tapping their feet, or being a fidgeter, stating they usually sit pretty still.
